balance-of-payments-s2.title: Five transactions for Belvia
balance-of-payments-s2.html:
Belvia is an invented country. During one year these transactions happen between its residents and the rest of the world:

  1. A Belvian winery ships wine to a store abroad and is paid for it.
  2. A Belvian family sends part of its wages to relatives who live abroad.
  3. A pension fund abroad buys Belvian government bonds.
  4. Belvian tourists pay for hotels during a vacation abroad.
  5. A Belvian carmaker buys a factory in another country.

fx-policy-changes-s1.title: Belvia's central bank raises rates
fx-policy-changes-s1.html: Belvia's central bank works in an ample-reserves framework. It raises the interest rate it pays on reserve balances, so Belvia's policy rate rises, and other interest rates in Belvia follow. Expected inflation does not change, so Belvia's real interest rates rise relative to those in Arland. Savers in Arland can buy bonds in either country. (Arland and Belvia are invented; Arland's currency is the arl and Belvia's is the bel.)

fx-net-exports-s2.title: Coffee, machines and a weaker bel
fx-net-exports-s2.html: The bel, Belvia's currency, depreciates against the arl, Arland's currency. Belvian farms sell coffee to Arland, priced in bels. Belvian factories buy machines from Arland, priced in arls. Belvia's economy is producing below full employment. (Arland, Belvia and their currencies are invented.)

real-rates-financial-flows-s1.title: Arland's loanable funds market after its government borrows more (Arland and its trading partner Belvia are invented)

real-rates-financial-flows-s2.title: Belvia's central bank lowers rates
real-rates-financial-flows-s2.html: Belvia's central bank works in an ample-reserves framework. To fight a recession, it lowers the interest rate it pays on reserve balances, so the policy rate and other interest rates in Belvia fall. Expected inflation stays the same, so Belvia's real interest rates fall relative to Arland's. Savers in both countries can buy assets in either one. (Arland and Belvia are invented; the arl and the bel are their currencies.)

items.q: Use the table. What is Arland's balance of trade in goods and services, in billions of arls? Write a deficit as a negative number.

mistakes.why: The size is right but the sign is not: imports (470) are larger than exports (420), so the balance is a deficit, written -50.
That is the balance on goods alone. The balance of trade in goods and services adds services: 120 exported and 90 imported.

items.q: Use the table. What is Arland's current account balance, in billions of arls? Write a deficit as a negative number.

mistakes.why: That is only the balance of trade. The current account also counts net income from abroad (+15) and net transfers (-25).
You subtracted Arland's purchases of foreign assets. Buying assets is recorded in the capital and financial account, not the current account.
You counted the income Arland received but not the 30 it paid to foreigners. Net income is 45 - 30 = 15.

items.q: Use the table. What is Arland's capital and financial account balance, in billions of arls? Write a deficit as a negative number.

mistakes.why: The two balances are opposite in sign, not equal: a current account deficit of 60 is matched by a capital and financial account surplus of +60.
That is only the outflow for foreign assets Arland bought. The balance also counts the Arland assets foreigners bought, and it must equal minus the current account balance: +60.

items.q: Use the table and your capital and financial account balance. What value of Arland assets did foreign residents buy that year, in billions of arls?

mistakes.why: You subtracted Arland's purchases instead of adding them back. The balance is F - 90 = 60, so F = 150.
That is the net balance. Foreign purchases are larger, because Arland residents also bought 90 billion arls of foreign assets: 60 + 90 = 150.

items.q: How is transaction 3, the pension fund buying Belvian government bonds, recorded in Belvia's balance of payments?
options: As a credit (+) in the capital and financial account
As a credit (+) in the current account, like an export
As a debit (-) in the capital and financial account
It is left out, since a bond is not a good or a service

items.q: Which transactions are recorded in Belvia's capital and financial account? Select all that apply.
options: 1, the wine sold abroad
2, the wages sent to relatives abroad
3, the bonds bought by the pension fund
4, the hotel stays abroad
5, the factory bought abroad

items.q: How is transaction 5, the carmaker buying a factory abroad, recorded?
options: As an import of goods, a debit in the current account
As a debit (-) in the capital and financial account
As a credit (+) in the capital and financial account
As income received from abroad in the current account

items.q: Suppose transactions 2 and 4 grow larger while nothing else in Belvia's current account changes. What must happen to Belvia's capital and financial account balance?
options: It rises by the same amount the current account falls
It falls by the same amount as the current account
It stays the same, since transfers and travel are not trade in assets
Belvia's government budget deficit rises by the same amount

items.q: What does a country's balance of payments record?
options: The government's tax revenue minus its spending in a year
The market value of the final goods and services produced in a year
Every transaction between the country's residents and the rest of the world
The total amount the country owes to foreign lenders

items.q: Belvia has a current account surplus of 35 billion bels this year. What is its capital and financial account balance?
options: A surplus of 35 billion bels
A deficit of 35 billion bels
Zero, because asset trades are not counted
It depends on the government budget balance

items.q: A headline reads "Arland's government deficit hits a record." A classmate says this means Arland imported more than it exported. Which response is best?
options: Correct: a government deficit and a trade deficit are the same number
Correct, because a government deficit is recorded in the current account
Not necessarily: a budget deficit is outlays above tax revenue, not imports above exports
Not necessarily, because a deficit is recorded in the capital and financial account

items.q: Firms in Arland pay interest to foreign holders of their bonds. How is the interest payment recorded in Arland's balance of payments?
options: As a debit in the current account (income paid abroad)
As a debit in the capital and financial account
As a credit in the current account (income received)
It is not recorded, because no good changes hands

items.q: A company based abroad builds a new factory in Arland. How does this enter Arland's balance of payments?
options: As an export of goods, a credit in the current account
As a debit in the current account, because the factory is foreign-owned
As a debit in the capital and financial account
As a credit in the capital and financial account

items.q: Arland's exports fall, while its imports, income and transfers stay the same. With nothing else changing, which is most likely?
options: Its current account balance falls and its capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount
Both balances fall by the same amount
Its current account balance stays the same, because imports did not change
Its government's budget balance falls by the amount exports fell

items.q: Put the steps in order to find a country's capital and financial account balance from a table of its transactions.
options: Subtract imports of goods and services from exports of goods and services to get the balance of trade
Add net income from abroad and net transfers to get the current account balance
Use current account + capital and financial account = 0 to get the capital and financial account balance
State whether each balance is a surplus (positive) or a deficit (negative)

items.q: Arland has a current account deficit of 80 billion arls. Build an answer that identifies its capital and financial account balance and explains why.

specific.frame: Arland's capital and financial account has ___, because ___.
specific.model: Arland's capital and financial account has a surplus of 80 billion arls, because the two accounts sum to zero: Arland pays for buying more from the rest of the world than it sells by selling 80 billion arls more of assets to foreigners (or borrowing from them) than it buys.

claim.label: The balance
options: a surplus of 80 billion arls
a deficit of 80 billion arls
a balance of zero

why.1: The two balances sum to zero, so they have opposite signs: a deficit of 80 is matched by a surplus of 80.
why.2: Only the sum of the two accounts is zero; each one alone can be in surplus or deficit.

because.label: Why
options: Arland pays for its extra purchases by selling assets to foreigners or borrowing from them
the government spends more than it collects in taxes
exports always equal imports in the long run

why.1: That describes a budget deficit, which is not part of the balance of payments.
why.2: Exports and imports need not be equal; the gap is what the asset sales pay for.

items.q: Which transaction belongs in a country's current account?
options: A resident buys shares in a foreign company
A foreign bank lends money to a local firm
A worker sends money home to family abroad
A foreigner buys a plot of land in the country

items.q: Use the table. In Year 2, what is the price of one bel in arls (arls per bel)?

mistakes.why: That is the price of the arl in bels, as the table gives it. The price of the bel in arls is the reciprocal: 1 / 2.5 = 0.4.

items.q: Use the table. What happened from Year 1 to Year 2?
options: The arl appreciated and the bel depreciated
The arl depreciated and the bel appreciated
Both currencies appreciated
Neither changed in value, since prices did not change

items.q: Use the table. In Year 3, a hotel in Belvia charges 300 bels a night. What does one night cost an Arland traveler, in arls?

mistakes.why: You multiplied the bel price by bels per arl, which gives bels squared per arl. Divide by 1.6 (or multiply by 0.625 arls per bel) to get arls.

items.q: Use the table. A Belvian good keeps the same price in bels from Year 2 to Year 3. What happens to its price for a buyer in Arland, in arls?
options: It falls, because the arl appreciated
It rises, because each arl buys fewer bels
It stays the same, because the bel price did not change
It falls, because each bel buys less of an arl

items.q: What did one bicycle cost the shop last year, in arls?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by bels per arl. To turn bels into arls, divide by the number of bels one arl buys: 800 / 4 = 200.

items.q: What does one bicycle cost the shop this year, in arls?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by bels per arl. Divide the bel price by 5 bels per arl: 800 / 5 = 160.
That is last year's cost at 4 bels per arl. This year one arl buys 5 bels.

items.q: Which describes the change in the exchange rate from last year to this year?
options: The arl depreciated against the bel
The bel appreciated against the arl
The arl appreciated against the bel
Neither, because the bicycle price in bels did not change

items.q: Which person is made worse off by this change in the exchange rate, other things equal?
options: A Belvian store buying goods priced in arls
The Arland bicycle shop
An Arland family vacationing in Belvia
A Belvian who keeps savings in arls

items.q: What is an exchange rate?
options: The interest rate a central bank pays on reserves
The price of one currency in units of another
A country's exports divided by its imports
The gap between two countries' inflation rates

items.q: A rate quoted as arls per bel rises from 0.40 to 0.50. What happened?
options: The arl appreciated against the bel
The bel depreciated against the arl
Nothing can be said without a quote in bels per arl
The bel appreciated against the arl

items.q: A concert ticket in Arland costs 60 arls. The exchange rate is 1.5 bels per arl. What does the ticket cost a visitor from Belvia, in bels?

mistakes.why: You divided. Each arl costs 1.5 bels, so 60 arls cost 60 times 1.5 = 90 bels.

items.q: The arl appreciates against the bel. Which statements follow? Select all that apply.
options: The number of bels per arl rises
The bel appreciates against the arl
The number of arls per bel rises
A Belvian good with an unchanged bel price costs fewer arls
An Arland good with an unchanged arl price costs fewer bels

items.q: An Arland student pays tuition in Belvia that is fixed in bels. Which change makes the semester cheaper for the student, in arls?
options: The rate moves from 4 bels per arl to 3 bels per arl
The rate moves from 3 bels per arl to 4 bels per arl
The rate moves from 0.25 arl per bel to 0.30 arl per bel
The tuition rises in bels while the rate stays the same

items.q: Put the steps in order to turn a price in bels into a price in arls.
options: Read the units of the quoted rate (bels per arl or arls per bel)
If the rate is in bels per arl, flip it to get arls per bel
Multiply the price in bels by arls per bel
Check that the units leave arls: bels times arls per bel gives arls

items.q: The rate moves from 2 bels per arl to 2.5 bels per arl. Student A says: "Bels per arl rose, so the arl got stronger." Student B says: "Arls per bel fell, so the bel got weaker." Who is right?
options: Student A, but Student B has the direction backward
Student B, but Student A has the direction backward
Both: they describe one change from its two sides
Neither: a higher rate means a weaker currency

items.q: The exchange rate moves from 2 bels per arl to 3 bels per arl. Build an answer that identifies which currency appreciated and explains how you know.

specific.model: The arl appreciated, because each arl now buys 3 bels instead of 2, which is more bels per arl; the bel depreciated, because each bel now buys one third of an arl instead of one half.

currency.label: Which currency
options: The arl
The bel

why.1: Each bel now buys one third of an arl instead of one half, less than before, so the bel depreciated.

because.label: How you know
options: each arl now buys more bels than before
each arl now buys fewer bels than before
the number in the quote got bigger, and a bigger number is a stronger currency

why.1: From 2 to 3 bels per arl, each arl buys more bels, not fewer.
why.2: A bigger number shows appreciation only for the currency the quote is "per"; flip the quote and the number gets smaller. Give the reason: what one unit buys.

items.q: The rate is 2.5 bels per arl. A traveler from Belvia trades 1,000 bels for arls. How many arls does the traveler get?
options: 2,500 arls
250 arls
1,000 arls
400 arls

items.q: What does the vertical axis of this graph measure?
options: The price of the bel, in arls per bel
The price of the arl, in bels per arl
The interest rate on Arland bonds
The price level in Arland

options: Arland residents who want to buy Belvian goods
Belvian firms that sell their goods inside Belvia

options: Arland residents who want Belvian goods, services or assets
Belvian tourists planning trips to Arland

items.q: Suppose the price of the arl were above its equilibrium on this graph. What would happen, and why?
options: A shortage of arls would push the price of the arl up further
The demand for arls would shift right until it met the price
A surplus of arls would push the price of the arl down

items.q: What happened to the international value of the arl?
options: It depreciated: each arl buys fewer bels
It appreciated: each arl buys more bels
It did not change, because supply did not shift

items.q: What is the matching change in the market for bels?
options: The supply of bels increases, and the bel depreciates
The demand for bels increases, and the bel appreciates
The supply of bels decreases, and the bel appreciates

items.q: Which event could have caused the shift shown?
options: Arland consumers buy more cheese imported from Belvia
Belvian tourists stop visiting Arland
Arland residents buy more Belvian bonds
Belvian consumers buy more phones made in Arland

items.q: What happened to the quantity of arls traded?
options: It fell, because the arl became more expensive
It stayed the same, since the price did the adjusting
It rose, along the supply curve

items.q: Label the axes and the curves of the market for arls, the currency of Arland, traded for bels.
Tourists from Belvia start visiting Arland in much larger numbers. In the market for arls, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: more Belvian tourists buying arls to spend in Arland

slips.S: Belvian tourists trade bels for arls, which is demand for arls. The supply of arls comes from Arland residents buying foreign things.

items.q: In the market for arls, mark a point on the supply curve where the price of the arl is higher than at the equilibrium.
Arland households buy more cheese imported from Belvia. Draw the market for bels, the currency of Belvia: label it, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: Arland households buying more Belvian cheese

slips.S: Arland households pay arls to get bels, so in the market for bels they demand bels. They supply arls only in the market for arls.

items.q: What happens in the foreign exchange market?
options: Central banks set the interest rates banks pay on reserves
Currencies are bought and sold, which sets exchange rates
Governments buy and sell goods across borders
Firms borrow by selling bonds to savers

items.q: Why does the demand curve for arls slope down?
options: When the arl is cheaper in bels, Arland goods cost Belvians fewer bels, so they want more arls
When the arl is cheaper, Arland residents want to sell more arls
When the arl is cheaper, Arland interest rates rise
When the arl is cheaper, Belvian goods cost Arland residents fewer arls

items.q: Arland residents increase their purchases of Belvian goods. What changes in the two currency markets?
options: Demand for arls rises, and supply of bels rises
Supply of arls falls, and demand for bels falls
Supply of arls rises, and demand for bels rises
Supply of arls rises, and the bel market does not change

items.q: Arland residents buy many more phones made in Belvia. Build the chain from this change to the value of the arl.

specific.frame: Arland buyers need bels, so ___ shifts ___, and the arl ___.
specific.model: Arland buyers need bels to pay for the phones, so they sell more arls: the supply of arls shifts to the right, and the arl depreciates because more arls are offered at every price while demand is unchanged, which lowers the price of the arl in bels.

curve.label: The curve
options: the supply of arls
the demand for arls

why.1: Demand for arls comes from Belvians who want Arland things. Arland buyers are sellers of arls.

direction.label: Which way
options: right
left

why.1: More arls are offered at every price, which is a shift to the right.

currency.label: The arl
options: depreciates
appreciates

why.1: More supply with the same demand lowers the price of the arl, so it depreciates.

items.q: Which of these add to the demand for arls in the foreign exchange market? Select all that apply.
options: A Belvian bakery buys wheat from an Arland farm
A Belvian saver buys bonds issued in Arland
An Arland tourist pays for a hotel in Belvia
An Arland firm buys a factory in Belvia
An Arland importer pays for cars from Belvia

items.q: What happens in the market for bels?
options: The supply of bels increases, so the bel depreciates
The demand for bels increases, so the bel appreciates
The demand for bels decreases, so the bel depreciates
Nothing changes, because interest rates are not traded

items.q: What is the matching change in the market for arls?
options: The supply of arls increases, so the arl depreciates
The demand for arls increases, so the arl appreciates
The supply of arls decreases, so the arl appreciates
The demand for arls decreases, so the arl appreciates

items.q: Which action by Arland savers links the higher Belvian interest rates to the currency markets?
options: They buy more Belvian goods for their homes
They save less, since Arland rates did not change
They use bels to buy more Arland bonds
They sell arls for bels to buy Belvian bonds

items.q: A student writes that Belvia's central bank raised rates by selling bonds on the open market. Why does that answer not fit this scenario?
options: Selling bonds is fiscal policy, set by the government
Selling bonds would lower interest rates, not raise them
With ample reserves, the bank moves its policy rate by changing administered rates such as interest on reserves
It fits: the two frameworks use the same tools

items.q: Considering only the change in inflation rates, what happens to the value of the arl against the bel?
options: It appreciates, because prices in Arland are higher
It does not change, since real rates are what move currencies
It depreciates, because Arland goods become relatively dearer
It appreciates, because Belvians need more arls for each Arland good

items.q: Considering only the change in real interest rates, what happens to the value of the arl?
options: It appreciates, as Belvian savers demand arls to buy Arland bonds
It depreciates, because borrowing in Arland costs more
It depreciates, as Arland savers buy Belvian bonds
It does not change, because nominal rates are not shown

items.q: Which changes in the table, each taken on its own, tend to make the arl depreciate? Select all that apply.
options: The rise in Arland's inflation rate
The rise in Arland's real interest rate
The faster growth of Arland's real GDP
The steady inflation rate in Belvia

items.q: All three changes in Arland happen at once. What can you conclude about the value of the arl?
options: It depreciates, because two of the three changes push it down
It appreciates, because interest rates outweigh the rest
It does not change, because the effects cancel out exactly
It is indeterminate: the changes push in opposite directions

items.q: Arland's central bank raises its policy rate to fight inflation, and expected inflation does not change, so Arland's real interest rates rise relative to Belvia's. In the market for arls, show the effect and mark the new equilibrium.

slips.S: Higher real interest rates in Arland make its assets more attractive: Belvians demand more arls, or Arland residents supply fewer arls to buy Belvian assets. Either raises the price of the arl; shifting supply right would lower it.

items.q: Real income in Arland rises faster than in Belvia, and Arland households buy more goods imported from Belvia. Draw the market for arls: label it, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: Arland households buying more imports as their incomes rise

slips.D: Rising Arland incomes change what Arland residents buy abroad, and they pay with arls: that is the supply of arls, not demand.

items.q: Arland's price level rises faster than Belvia's. In the market for arls, show the effect and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: higher inflation in Arland than in Belvia

items.q: In the market for arls, mark a point on the demand curve where the price of the arl is lower than at the equilibrium.
Arland's central bank works in an ample-reserves framework and wants to tighten policy. Build the chain from its action to the value of the arl.

specific.frame: The central bank ___; interest rates in Arland ___; ___ shifts right; the arl ___.
specific.model: The central bank raises the interest rate it pays on reserve balances, so the policy rate and other Arland interest rates rise. Because Arland's real interest rates are now higher relative to Belvia's, Belvian savers buy more Arland bonds, so the demand for arls shifts right and the arl appreciates.

tool.label: The action
options: raises the interest rate it pays on reserve balances
sells government bonds on the open market
raises income taxes

why.1: Selling bonds is the limited-reserves tool; the question sets ample reserves, where the bank changes administered rates.
why.2: Taxes are fiscal policy, set by the government, not a central bank tool.

rate.label: Interest rates
options: rise
fall

why.1: Tightening raises the policy rate and the rates that follow it.

curve.label: The curve
options: the demand for arls
the supply of arls

why.1: Foreign savers buying Arland bonds need arls: they demand arls. (Arland savers keeping funds at home would, if anything, supply fewer arls.)

currency.label: The arl
options: appreciates
depreciates

why.1: More demand for arls raises their price in bels: the arl appreciates.

items.q: Arland's government raises spending and pays for it by borrowing, so it runs a larger budget deficit. Through the loanable funds market, what happens to the arl?
options: It appreciates: the real interest rate rises, so foreign savers want Arland bonds
It depreciates: a budget deficit makes Arland poorer
It depreciates: the real interest rate falls as the government spends
Nothing happens, because a budget deficit is not a trade deficit

items.q: Arland's central bank works in a limited-reserves framework and buys government bonds on the open market. What happens to the arl, other things equal?
options: It appreciates, because the central bank is buying
It depreciates, because Arland interest rates fall
It does not change, because bond purchases are domestic
It depreciates, because Arland inflation falls

items.q: Currency traders come to expect that the bel will appreciate against the arl next month. What happens in the market for bels now?
options: Demand for bels falls, since traders wait for next month
Supply of bels rises, so the bel depreciates now
Nothing happens until the appreciation arrives
Demand for bels rises now, so the bel appreciates now

items.q: Consumers in Belvia lose interest in cars made in Arland and buy fewer of them. What happens in the market for arls?
options: Demand for arls falls, so the arl depreciates
Supply of arls falls, so the arl appreciates
Demand for arls rises, so the arl appreciates
Supply of arls rises, so the arl depreciates

items.q: Use the table. What were Arland's net exports in the year before the appreciation, in billions of arls?

mistakes.why: Net exports are exports minus imports, not imports minus exports: 500 - 450 = +50.

items.q: Use the table. By how much did Arland's net exports change from the year before to the year after, in billions of arls? Write a decrease as a negative number.

mistakes.why: That is the level of net exports after the appreciation. The change subtracts the level before: -20 - 50 = -70.
The size is right, but net exports fell, so the change is negative: -70.

items.q: Use the table. Other things equal, what happens to Arland's aggregate demand?
options: It shifts right, because exports are still large
It does not shift, because imports are not part of GDP
It shifts left, because net exports fell
Short-run aggregate supply shifts left instead

items.q: Arland trades with Belvia alone. What happened to Belvia's net exports?
options: They fell, along with Arland's
They did not change, since the arl changed value
They fell, because Belvian goods became dearer
They rose by the amount Arland's fell

items.q: What happens to Belvia's coffee exports to Arland, other things equal?
options: They rise, because Belvian coffee costs fewer arls
They fall, because each bel is worth less
They do not change, because the bel price is unchanged
They fall, because coffee costs Arland buyers more arls

items.q: What happens to Belvian factories' purchases of machines from Arland, other things equal?
options: They rise, because the machines are cheaper in bels
They fall, because each machine costs more bels
They do not change, because the arl price is unchanged
They rise, because Belvia exports more coffee

items.q: Putting both effects together, what happens to Belvia's aggregate demand?
options: It shifts left, because the bel lost value
It does not shift, because the two effects cancel
It shifts right, because net exports rise
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right instead

items.q: In the short run, what happens to Belvia's real output and unemployment?
